Monks, if shame and fear of wrongdoing are present, for a monk who is possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, the proximate cause for the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled. If the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties is present, for a monk who is possessed of the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, the proximate cause for the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is fulfilled. If the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is present, for a monk who is possessed of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, the proximate cause for right concentration is fulfilled. If right concentration is present, for a monk who is possessed of right concentration, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is fulfilled. If the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is present, for a monk who is possessed of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment and dispassion is fulfilled. If disenchantment and dispassion are present, for a monk who is possessed of disenchantment and dispassion, the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahantship and the reviewing knowledge that reflects upon the fruit of Arahantship is fulfilled. Monks, just as when a tree is possessed of branches and leaves, its scaly bark reaches fullness, and its bark, its softwood, and its heartwood reach fullness. In the same way, monks, if shame and fear of wrongdoing are present, for a monk who is possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, the proximate cause for the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled. ... [Pe] ... the reviewing knowledge that reflects upon the fruit of Arahantship is also fulfilled.

The First Sutta.

## 2. Sattasūriya Sutta
66. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
474:
The Blessed One said this:
Monks, conditioned things are impermanent. Monks, conditioned things are unstable. Monks, conditioned things provide no solace. Monks, it is enough to be weary of all conditioned things, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.

Monks, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length, eighty-four thousand yojanas in width, eighty-four thousand yojanas submerged in the great ocean, and eighty-four thousand yojanas rising above the great ocean.

Monks, there comes a time when, after a long period has passed, it does not rain for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years. There is indeed such a time when it does not rain. Monks, when it does not rain, all the seeds and vegetation, the medicinal plants, the grasses, and the forest trees dry up, wither away, and exist no more. Monks, conditioned things are thus impermanent. Monks, conditioned things are thus unstable... [Pe] ...enough to be liberated.

Monks, there comes a time when, after a long period has passed, a second sun appears. There is indeed such a time when two suns appear. Monks, with the appearance of the second sun, all the small rivers and small lakes dry up, wither away, and exist no more (not even a drop of water remains). Monks, conditioned things are thus impermanent... [Pe] ...enough to be liberated.

Monks, there comes a time when, after a long period has passed, (after the appearance of the second sun), a third sun appears. There is indeed such a time when three suns appear. Monks, with the appearance of the third sun, all the five great rivers—namely, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—dry up, wither away, and exist no more. Monks, conditioned things are thus impermanent... [Pe] ...enough to be liberated.

Monks, there comes a time when, after a long period has passed, (after the appearance of the third sun), a fourth sun appears. There is indeed such a time when four suns appear. Monks, with the appearance of the fourth sun, those great lakes from which the great rivers flow—namely, Anotatta, Sīhapapāta, Rathakāra, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Kuṇāla, Chaddanta, and Mandākinī—these seven great lakes dry up, wither away, and exist no more. Monks, conditioned things are thus impermanent... [Pe] ...enough to be liberated.

Monks, there comes a time when, after a long period has passed, (after the appearance of the fourth sun), a fifth sun appears. There is indeed such a time when five suns appear.
475:
Monks, with the appearance of the fifth sun, the waters in the great ocean recede by a hundred yojanas, by two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, five hundred yojanas, six hundred yojanas, and by seven hundred yojanas. The water in the great ocean remains at a depth of seven palm trees, six palm trees, five palm trees, four palm trees, three palm trees, two palm trees, and even just one palm tree. The water in the great ocean remains at a depth of seven men's heights, six men's heights, five men's heights, four men's heights, three men's heights, two men's heights, one man's height, half a man's height, waist-deep, knee-deep, and even just ankle-deep. Monks, just as in the autumn season when it rains heavily with large drops, water stands here and there in the footprints of cows; even so, monks, the water in the great ocean stands here and there only ankle-deep. Monks, with the appearance of the fifth sun, there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet a finger-joint. So impermanent, monks, are formations... [it is] enough to be liberated [from them].

There comes a time, monks, at some point after a long period, when the sixth sun appears. With the appearance of the sixth sun, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, smoke, smolder, and billow with smoke. Monks, just as a potter's kiln, when first fired, smokes, smolders, and billows with smoke; even so, monks, with the appearance of the sixth sun, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, smoke, smolder, and billow with smoke. So impermanent, monks, are formations... [it is] enough to be liberated [from them].

There comes a time, monks, at some point after a long period, when the seventh sun appears. With the appearance of the seventh sun, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, burst into flames, blaze up, and become one mass of flame. Monks, of this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, as they are burning and consuming, the flame, tossed by the wind, reaches even to the Brahma world. Monks, as Sineru, the king of mountains, is burning, consuming, and perishing, overcome by the great mass of fire, its peaks of a hundred yojanas crumble and perish.
476:
Its peaks of two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, and five hundred yojanas also crumble and perish. Monks, of this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, as they are burning and consuming, neither ash nor soot is found. Monks, just as when ghee or oil is burning and consuming, neither ash nor soot is found; even so, monks, of this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, as they are burning and consuming, neither ash nor soot is found. So impermanent, monks, are formations; so unstable, monks, are formations; so unreliable, monks, are formations. This is enough, monks, to become weary of all formations, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated.

In this matter, monks, who would know, who would believe—except those who have seen the state [of Nibbāna]—that 'this earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn, will perish, and will be no more'?

Monks, in the past, there was a teacher named Sunetta, a sect-founder, who was free from lust for sensual pleasures. Monks, the teacher Sunetta had many hundreds of disciples. Monks, the teacher Sunetta taught his disciples the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world. Monks, when the teacher Sunetta was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world, those who completely understood his teaching in its entirety, with the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in a good destination, the Brahma world. Those who did not completely understand the teaching in its entirety, with the breaking up of the body, after death, some were reborn in companionship with the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas, some with the Nimmānarati devas, some with the Tusita devas, some with the Yāma devas, some with the Tāvatimsa devas, some with the Cātumahārājika devas, some in companionship with wealthy Khattiyas, some with wealthy Brāhmaṇas, and some in companionship with wealthy householders.

Monks, then this thought occurred to the teacher Sunetta: 'It is not fitting for me to have the same destination in the next life as my disciples. What if I were to develop mettā (loving-kindness) [to a higher degree]?'

Monks, then the teacher Sunetta developed a mind of mettā for seven years, and for seven aeons of world-contraction and world-expansion, he did not return to this world.
477:
Monks, when the world is contracting, he reaches the Ābhassara Brahma realm. When the world is expanding, he is reborn in an empty Brahma palace of the first jhāna. Monks, in that Brahma palace, he becomes the Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā), the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-seeing, the Wielder of Power.

Monks, he became Sakka, the King of the Gods, thirty-six times. More than a hundred times, he was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), a righteous king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters, who had established stability in the country and possessed the seven treasures. He had more than a thousand sons who were heroic, of mighty stature, and capable of crushing enemy armies. He ruled over this earth, bounded by the ocean, without rod or weapon, conquering by Dhamma alone.

Monks, although the teacher Sunetta lived so long and remained for such a long time, I say that he was not free from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he was not free from suffering. Why is that? It is because of not understanding and not penetrating four things. What are the four?

Monks, through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Virtue (Sīla), one is not free from the mass of suffering.
Through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Concentration (Samādhi), one is not free from the mass of suffering.
Through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Wisdom (Paññā), one is not free from the mass of suffering.
Through not understanding and not penetrating Noble Liberation (Vimutti), one is not free from the mass of suffering.

Monks, I have understood and penetrated this Noble Virtue. I have understood and penetrated Noble Concentration. I have understood and penetrated Noble Wisdom. I have understood and penetrated Noble Liberation. Craving for existence has been cut off; the cord that leads to existence is exhausted. Now, there is no more rebirth.

The Blessed One spoke these words. Having said this, the Teacher, the Sugata, further spoke these verses:

"Virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation—
These things have been understood by the renowned Gotama.

Thus, having known them through direct knowledge, the Buddha taught the Dhamma to the monks.
The Teacher, the end-maker of suffering, the One with Vision, has attained Parinibbāna (with the extinguishing of defilements)." (Second Sutta).
478:
Second Sutta.

## 3. Nagaroppama Sutta

67. Monks, when a king's frontier fortress is well-guarded by seven fortifications and obtains the four kinds of food/provisions as much as desired, without difficulty and without hardship, then that frontier fortress of the king is said to be impregnable by external enemies and foes. By what seven fortifications is it well-guarded?

Monks, in this world, in the king's frontier fortress, there is a pillar (esikā) with deep foundations, well-planted, immovable, and unshakable. With this first fortification, the king's frontier fortress is well-guarded for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. (1)

Furthermore, monks, in the king's frontier fortress, there is a moat (parikhā) that is both deep and wide. With this second fortification, the king's frontier fortress is well-guarded for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. (2)

Furthermore, monks, in the king's frontier fortress, there is an encircling road (anupariyāyapatha) that is both high and wide. With this third fortification, the king's frontier fortress is well-guarded for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. (3)

Furthermore, monks, in the king's frontier fortress, many weapons (āvudha) are stored, both those to be launched (like arrows) and other weapons (like swords). With this fourth fortification, the king's frontier fortress is well-guarded for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. (4)

Furthermore, monks, in the king's frontier fortress, a large army (balakāya) resides. What kind of army? Elephant riders, horse riders, chariot warriors, archers, standard-bearers, battle-arrayers, those who can enter the enemy army and cut off heads, noble princes of great renown, chargers, heroes like great elephants, the extremely brave, leather-clad warriors, and loyal servants. With this fifth fortification, the king's frontier fortress is well-guarded for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. (5)

Furthermore, monks, in the king's frontier fortress, there is a gatekeeper (dovārika) who is wise, experienced, and intelligent, who keeps out strangers and lets in those who are known.
479:
There is a gatekeeper who keeps out strangers and admits those who are known. For the protection of those within and the warding off of those without, the king's frontier city is well-guarded by this sixth city safeguard. (6)

Furthermore, bhikkhus, in the king's frontier city, there is a wall, high and wide, and well-finished with plaster. For the protection of those within and the warding off of those without, the king's frontier city is well-guarded by this seventh city safeguard. (7)

The city is well-guarded by these seven city safeguards.

What are the four types of provisions that are obtained at will, without difficulty, and without trouble?

Bhikkhus, here in the king's frontier city, much grass, wood, and water are stored for the delight, security, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without. (1)

Furthermore, bhikkhus, in the king's frontier city, much rice and barley are stored for the delight, security, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without. (2)

Furthermore, bhikkhus, in the king's frontier city, much sesame, mung beans, black grams, and other pulses are stored for the delight, security, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without. (3)

Furthermore, bhikkhus, in the king's frontier city, much medicine is stored for the delight, security, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without. What medicines? Namely: ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, and salt. These are the medicines.

Bhikkhus, these four types of provisions are obtained at will, without difficulty, and without trouble. (4)

Bhikkhus, when a king's frontier city is well-guarded by these seven city safeguards and obtains these four types of provisions at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, then that frontier city is said to be invincible to external enemies and foes.

In the same way, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple is possessed of seven good qualities (saddhamma) and obtains at will the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life...
480:
...obtains them without difficulty and without trouble. Bhikkhus, then this noble disciple is said to be one who cannot be overcome by Māra, cannot be overcome by the Evil One.

With what seven good qualities is he possessed?

Just as, bhikkhus, in a king's frontier city, there is a pillar (esikā) with deep foundations, well-planted, unshakable, and unmoving, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without; in the same way, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has faith. He has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One... [pe] ... the Buddha, the Blessed One.'

Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who has faith as his pillar abandons what is unwholesome and develops what is wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this first good quality. (1)

Just as, bhikkhus, in a king's frontier city, there is a moat (parikkhā), both deep and wide, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without; in the same way, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has a sense of shame (hirī). He is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is ashamed of falling into evil, unwholesome states. Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who has shame as his moat abandons what is unwholesome and develops what is wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this second good quality. (2)

Just as, bhikkhus, in a king's frontier city, there is an encircling road (anupariyāyapatha), both high and wide, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without; in the same way, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has a fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). He fears bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he fears falling into evil, unwholesome states. Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who has fear of wrongdoing as his encircling road abandons what is unwholesome and develops what is wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this third good quality. (3)

Just as, bhikkhus, in a king's frontier city, many weapons (āvudha) are stored, both those for throwing and those for other uses, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without; in the same way, bhikkhus, the noble disciple is one of great learning... [pe] ... well-penetrated by wisdom. Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who has learning as his weapon...
481:
Monks, the learned noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons blameworthy states and develops blameless states; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this fourth true quality. (4)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city there dwells a large body of troops—namely, elephant riders, cavalry, charioteers, archers, standard-bearers, camp-followers, those who deal heavy blows to the enemy, formidable warriors, princes, chargers, great elephant-like warriors, heroes, leather-clad warriors, and sons of loyal slaves—for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple lives with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, and does not lay down the burden in regard to wholesome states. Monks, the noble disciple who is possessed of the strength of energy abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons blameworthy states and develops blameless states; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this fifth true quality. (5)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city there is a gatekeeper who is wise, experienced, and intelligent, who keeps out strangers and lets in acquaintances, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and prudence, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. Monks, the noble disciple who has mindfulness as a gatekeeper abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons blameworthy states and develops blameless states; he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this sixth true quality. (6)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city there is a wall that is high and wide, with all gaps closed and plastered with mortar, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple is wise, possessing wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the right destruction of suffering.

Monks, the noble disciple who is endowed with the mortar-plaster of wisdom abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons blameworthy states and develops blameless states;
482:
he maintains himself in purity. He is possessed of this seventh true quality. He is possessed of these seven true qualities. (7)

Which are the four jhānas, pertaining to the higher mind, providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life, that he obtains at will, without difficulty, without hardship?

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city a large store of grass, wood, and water is collected for the delight, security, and comfort of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple, for his own delight, security, and comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. (1)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city a large store of rice and barley is collected for the delight, security, and comfort of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple, for his own delight, security, and comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna, with the stilling of thought and examination... enters and dwells in the second jhāna. (2)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city a large store of sesame, mung beans, kidney beans, and other pulses is collected for the delight, security, and comfort of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple, for his own delight, security, and comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. (3)

Monks, just as in a king’s frontier city a large store of medicines is collected—namely, ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, and salt—for the delight, security, and comfort of those within and to ward off those without; in the same way, monks, the noble disciple, for his own delight, security, and comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

He obtains these four jhānas, pertaining to the higher mind, providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life, at will, without difficulty, without hardship. (4)

Monks, when a noble disciple is possessed of these seven true qualities and obtains these four jhānas, pertaining to the higher mind, providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life, at will, without difficulty, without hardship;

Monks, then this noble disciple is called a monk whom Māra cannot do with as he pleases,
483:
“Bhikkhus, this is called a noble disciple whom the Evil Māra cannot do with as he wishes.”

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Dhammaññū Sutta

68. “Bhikkhus, a monk endowed with seven qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. 

What are the seven?

Bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, a monk is one who knows the Dhamma (the texts), knows the meaning, knows himself, knows moderation, knows the right time, knows the assembly, and knows the difference between individuals.

And how, bhikkhus, is a monk one who knows the Dhamma? 

Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows the Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know the Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya... [as before] ...and Vedalla, he would not be called ‘one who knows the Dhamma’ in this Dispensation. But because, bhikkhus, a monk knows the Dhamma—the Sutta, Geyya... and Vedalla, he is called ‘one who knows the Dhamma’ (Dhammaññū). Thus, he knows the Dhamma. (1)

And how is he one who knows the meaning? Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows the meaning of this or that statement: ‘This is the meaning of that statement; this is the meaning of that statement.’ If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know the meaning of this or that statement: ‘This is the meaning of that statement; this is the meaning of that statement,’ he would not be called ‘one who knows the meaning’ in this Dispensation. But because, bhikkhus, a monk knows the meaning of this or that statement: ‘This is the meaning of that statement; this is the meaning of that statement,’ he is called ‘one who knows the meaning’ (Atthaññū). Thus, he knows the Dhamma and knows the meaning. (2)

And how is he one who knows himself? 

Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows himself: ‘I have this much faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and ready wit (paṭibhāna).’ If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know himself: ‘I have this much faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and ready wit,’ he would not be called ‘one who knows himself’ in this Dispensation.
484:
Bhikkhus, because a monk knows himself: ‘I have this much faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and ready wit,’ he is called ‘one who knows himself’ (Attaññū). Thus, he knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, and knows himself. (3)

And how is he one who knows moderation? 

Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows moderation in receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know moderation in receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites, he would not be called ‘one who knows moderation’ in this Dispensation. But because, bhikkhus, a monk knows moderation in receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites, he is called ‘one who knows moderation’ (Mattaññū). Thus, he knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, and knows moderation. (4)

And how is he one who knows the right time? 

Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows the time: ‘This is the time for recitation; this is the time for questioning; this is the time for exertion; this is the time for seclusion.’ If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know the time: ‘This is the time for recitation; this is the time for questioning; this is the time for exertion; this is the time for seclusion,’ he would not be called ‘one who knows the time’ in this Dispensation. But because, bhikkhus, a monk knows the time: ‘This is the time for recitation; this is the time for questioning; this is the time for exertion; this is the time for seclusion,’ he is called ‘one who knows the time’ (Kālaññū). 

Thus, he knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows moderation, and knows the time. (5)

And how is he one who knows the assembly? 

Here, bhikkhus, a monk knows the assembly: ‘This is an assembly of Khattiyas; this is an assembly of Brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of recluses. In that assembly, one should approach in this way, stand in this way, act in this way, sit in this way, speak in this way, or remain silent in this way.’ If, bhikkhus, a monk did not know the assembly: ‘This is an assembly of Khattiyas... [as before] ...or remain silent in this way,’ he would not be called ‘one who knows the assembly’ in this world. But because, bhikkhus, he knows: ‘This is an assembly of Khattiyas, an assembly of Brahmins, an assembly of householders, an assembly of recluses; in that assembly, one should approach in this way, stand in this way, act in this way, sit in this way, speak in this way, or remain silent in this way,’ he is called ‘one who knows the assembly’ (Parisaññū).

Thus, he knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows moderation, knows the time, and knows the assembly. (6)

And how is he one who knows the difference between individuals (the high and the low)? 

Here, bhikkhus, individuals are known by a monk in two ways. Of two persons, one desires to see the noble ones, and one does not desire to see the noble ones.
485:
A person does not desire to see the Noble Ones. A person who does not desire to see the Noble Ones is blameworthy for that reason. A person who desires to see the Noble Ones is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who desire to see the Noble Ones, one desires to hear the True Dhamma, and one does not desire to hear the True Dhamma. The one who does not desire to hear the True Dhamma is blameworthy for that reason. The one who desires to hear the True Dhamma is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who desire to hear the True Dhamma, one listens to the Dhamma attentively, and one listens to the Dhamma inattentively. The one who listens inattentively is blameworthy for that reason. The one who listens attentively is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who listen to the Dhamma attentively, one retains the Dhamma after hearing it, and one does not retain the Dhamma after hearing it. The one who does not retain the Dhamma is blameworthy for that reason. The one who retains the Dhamma is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who retain the Dhamma after hearing it, one examines the meaning of the retained Dhamma, and one does not examine the meaning of the retained Dhamma. The one who does not examine the meaning is blameworthy for that reason. The one who examines the meaning is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who examine the meaning of the retained Dhamma, one understands the meaning and the text and practices in accordance with the Dhamma. One understands the meaning and the text but does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. The one who does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma is blameworthy for that reason. The one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma is praiseworthy for that reason.

Among two persons who understand the meaning and the text and practice in accordance with the Dhamma, one practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others. One practices for both his own benefit and
486:
the benefit of others. The one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others is blameworthy for that reason. The one who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others is praiseworthy for that reason.

Bhikkhus, in this way, a bhikkhu knows persons in two ways.

Bhikkhus, in this way, a bhikkhu knows the superiority and inferiority of persons.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these seven qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Pāricchattaka Sutta

69. Bhikkhus, at the time when the Pāricchattaka Kovilāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has pale yellow leaves;

Bhikkhus, at that time, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted and joyful, thinking:
"Now our Pāricchattaka Kovilāra tree has pale yellow leaves; soon the leaves will fall." (1)

Bhikkhus, at that time, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted and joyful, thinking:

## 8. Aggikkhandhopama Sutta

72. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country together with a large community of monks. While the Blessed One was wandering, he saw in a certain place a great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing. Having seen it, he stepped off the road and sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, do you see this great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing?"

"Yes, Bhante," they replied.

"Monks, what do you think? Which is better: that one should embrace and sit or lie down beside this great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing; or that one should embrace and sit or lie down beside a maiden of the warrior-noble caste, or a maiden of the brahmin caste, or a maiden of the householder class, with soft and tender hands and feet?"

"Bhante, it is better to embrace and sit or lie down beside a maiden of the warrior-noble caste, or a maiden of the brahmin caste, or a maiden of the householder class, with soft and tender hands and feet. For, Bhante, it is painful to embrace and sit or lie down beside this great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing."

"Monks, I declare to you, I announce to you: for one who is immoral, of evil nature, of impure and suspicious behavior, of concealed actions, who is not an ascetic but claims to be an ascetic, who is not a celibate but claims to be a celibate, who is rotten within, leaking, and full of refuse—for such a person, it is better to embrace and sit or lie down beside this great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing.

Why is that?

Monks, because on that account, that monk might meet death or death-like suffering, but he would not, on that account, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, or hell. But, monks, for that immoral person of evil nature, of impure and suspicious behavior... (p)... leaking, and full of refuse, who embraces and sits or lie down beside a maiden of the warrior-noble caste, or a maiden of the brahmin caste, or a maiden of the householder class, with soft and tender hands and feet—that, monks, will be for his harm and suffering for a long time; with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, or hell. (1)

Monks, what do you think? Suppose a strong man were to wrap both calves with a firm, strong horsehair rope and rub them. That horsehair rope would cut the outer skin; having cut the outer skin, it would cut the inner skin; having cut the inner skin, it would cut the flesh;"

“Monks, I declare to you, I inform you. For that immoral person of evil character ... who is refuse-like (kasambujāta), it is better that a strong man should bind both calves with a tough horsehair rope ... and remain touching the marrow.

Which is better: that a strong man, seizing one by the feet and holding one head down, should plunge one into a red-hot copper cauldron, glowing, blazing, and radiant—where one is cooked in the swirling foam, going now up, now down, and now across—or that one should enjoy a monastery given out of faith by wealthy Khattiyas, wealthy Brahmins, or wealthy Householders?”

“Venerable Sir, it would be better to enjoy a monastery given out of faith by wealthy Khattiyas, wealthy Brahmins, or wealthy Householders. “I tell you, bhikkhus, I declare to you, bhikkhus, that for an immoral person of evil character... who is like a heap of refuse, it would be better for a strong man to seize him by the feet and hold him head down... and go now across. 

Why is that? Because for that reason, bhikkhus, he might meet death or death-like suffering, but he would not, on that account, at the breaking up of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, or hell. But for an immoral person of evil character... who is like a heap of refuse, to enjoy a monastery given out of faith by wealthy Khattiyas, wealthy Brahmins, or wealthy Householders—”
500:
“—to enjoy that, bhikkhus, leads to his harm and suffering for a long time; at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, or hell. (7)

Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘The robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick that we use—the services of those donors shall be of great fruit and great benefit; and this going forth of ours shall not be barren, but fruitful and productive.’ 

Bhikkhus, this is how you should train yourselves. Bhikkhus, one who sees his own benefit is fit to strive with diligence. 

Bhikkhus, one who sees the benefit of others is fit to strive with diligence. 

Bhikkhus, one who sees the benefit of both is fit to strive with diligence.”

The Blessed One said this. While this exposition was being delivered, hot blood vomited from the mouths of sixty monks. ## 9. Sunetta Sutta

73. “Bhikkhus, in the past there was a teacher named Sunetta, a founder of a sect, who was free from lust for sensual pleasures. Bhikkhus, the teacher Sunetta had many hundreds of disciples. The teacher Sunetta taught his disciples the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world. Bhikkhus, when the teacher Sunetta was teaching the Dhamma for companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who did not have confidence in their hearts, at the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, or hell. Bhikkhus, when the teacher Sunetta was teaching the Dhamma for companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who had confidence in their hearts, at the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.

Bhikkhus, in the past there was a teacher named Mūgapakkha... a teacher named Aranemi... a teacher named Kuddālaka... a teacher named Hatthipāla... a teacher named Jotipāla... Bhikkhus, in the past there was a teacher named Araka, a founder of a sect, who was free from lust for sensual pleasures. Bhikkhus, the teacher Araka had many hundreds of disciples. The teacher Araka taught his disciples the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world.”
501:
Monks, when the teacher Araka taught the Dhamma for the sake of attaining the Brahma world, those disciples who did not have a settled mind in him, with the breaking up of the body after death, were reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. Monks, when the teacher Araka taught the Dhamma for the sake of attaining the Brahma world, those disciples who had a settled mind in him, with the breaking up of the body after death, were reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.

Monks, what do you think? If someone, with a corrupted mind, were to revile and abuse these seven teachers, founders of sects, who were free from lust, who had hundreds of followers, and who were accompanied by a community of disciples, would he not produce much demerit?

"Yes, Bhante."

Monks, if someone, with a corrupted mind, were to revile and abuse these seven teachers, founders of sects, who were free from lust, who had hundreds of followers, and who were accompanied by a community of disciples, he would produce much demerit. However, if someone, with a corrupted mind, reviles and abuses a single person endowed with right view (one who has attained the path of stream-entry), he produces even more demerit than that.

Why is that?

Monks, I do not speak of such tolerance outside [this teaching] as I do among fellow practitioners. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Our minds will not be corrupted towards our fellow practitioners.' Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Araka Sutta

74. Monks, in the past, there was a teacher named Araka, a founder of a sect, who was free from lust. Monks, the teacher Araka had many hundreds of disciples. The teacher Araka taught the Dhamma to his disciples in this way:

"O Brahmin, the life of human beings is short, limited, and fleeting; it has much suffering and much despair. It should be understood with wisdom; one should do what is wholesome and lead the holy life. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying."

"O Brahmin, for example, a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass quickly disappears when the sun rises;"
502:
it does not last long. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a dewdrop; it is short, limited, and fleeting; it has much suffering and much despair. It should be understood with wisdom; one should do what is wholesome and lead the holy life. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, when it is raining heavily, a water bubble on the surface of the water quickly disappears and does not last long. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a water bubble; it is short, limited, and fleeting; it has much suffering and much despair. It should be understood with wisdom; one should do what is wholesome and lead the holy life. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, a line drawn on the water with a stick quickly disappears and does not last long. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a line drawn on the water; it is short... (as above)... For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, a mountain river coming from afar, flowing swiftly, carrying debris along, has no moment, no second (laya), no minute (muhutta) that it turns back; rather, that river just goes, flows, and continues. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a mountain river; it is short, limited, and fleeting... (as above)... For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, just as a strong man might collect a glob of spit on the tip of his tongue and spit it out without effort. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a glob of spit; it is short, limited, and fleeting... (as above)... For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, if a piece of meat is thrown into an iron pan that has been heated all day, it quickly disappears and does not last long. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a piece of meat; it is short, limited, and fleeting... (as above)... For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

O Brahmin, for another example, a cow led to the slaughterhouse, with every step she takes, she is closer to the slaughter, closer to death. O Brahmin, even so, the life of human beings is like a cow led to the slaughter;
503:
“...It is short, it is fleeting, it has much suffering, it has much despair; it should be understood with wisdom, merit should be performed, the holy life should be lived; for one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.”

Monks, at that time, the lifespan of humans was sixty thousand years. A girl of five hundred years was fit for marriage. Monks, at that time, humans had only six types of diseases: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination. Monks, even though that teacher named Araka lived among humans who were so long-lived, so long-enduring, and had so few diseases, he still taught his disciples: “O Brahmin, the life of humans is meager, it is short, it is fleeting, it has much suffering, it has much despair; it should be understood with wisdom, merit should be performed, the holy life should be lived; for one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.”

Monks, if one were to say: “The life of humans is meager, it is short, it is fleeting, it has much suffering, it has much despair; it should be understood with wisdom, merit should be performed, the holy life should be lived; for one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying,” it is only now that such a statement would be well-spoken.

Monks, nowadays, one who lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little less, or a little more.

Monks, one who lives for a hundred years lives only for three hundred seasons: a hundred seasons of winter, a hundred seasons of summer, and a hundred seasons of the rains.

Monks, one who lives for three hundred seasons lives only for one thousand two hundred months: four hundred months of winter, four hundred months of summer, and four hundred months of the rains.

Monks, one who lives for one thousand two hundred months lives only for two thousand four hundred fortnights: eight hundred fortnights of winter, eight hundred fortnights of summer, and eight hundred fortnights of the rains.

Monks, one who lives for two thousand four hundred fortnights lives only for thirty-six thousand nights: twelve thousand nights of winter, twelve thousand nights of summer, and twelve thousand nights of the rains.

Monks, one who lives for thirty-six thousand nights eats only seventy-two thousand meals, including the time of nursing from the mother's breast and including interruptions to meals: twenty-four thousand meals in winter, twenty-four thousand meals in summer, and twenty-four thousand meals in the rains.

In this regard, these are the interruptions to eating:

One who is drowsy does not eat a meal; one who is in pain does not eat a meal; one who is sick does not eat a meal;
504:
One who observes the Uposatha does not eat a meal; one who does not obtain food does not eat a meal. These are the interruptions to eating.

Thus, monks, I have calculated the life of a human who lives a hundred years, I have calculated the lifespan, I have calculated the seasons, I have calculated the years, I have calculated the months, I have calculated the fortnights, I have calculated the nights, I have calculated the days, I have calculated the meals, and I have calculated the interruptions to meals.

Monks, what should be done by a teacher seeking the welfare of his disciples, out of compassion, has been done by me for you.

Monks, these are the roots of trees, these are empty huts. Meditate, monks! Do not be negligent! Do not be remorseful later! This is my instruction to you.

The Tenth Sutta.

The Seventh Chapter, the Great Chapter (Mahāvagga), is finished.
